title: OneDB: A Distributed Multi-Metric Data Similarity Search System

problem.claim: Retrieving multi-modal data effectively is difficult because user retrieval intents are diverse and dynamic.

gap.claim: Existing vector databases commonly rely on static embeddings or fixed weights and do not adapt to varying user preferences across modalities.

contributions.claim: OneDB is a distributed framework for multi-metric similarity search that integrates data management with learning-based techniques.
OneDB uses lightweight contrastive learning to adaptively infer metric weights and implicit user preferences from limited query examples.
OneDB combines global partitioning, modality-aware local indexing, and deep-reinforcement-learning-based parameter tuning to support heterogeneous data distributions and dynamic environments.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors explicitly distinguish three key algorithmic innovations in OneDB.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Experiments on real-world datasets reportedly show 12.63%--30.75% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art vector search systems.
Experiments reportedly show 2.5--5.75× faster retrieval speeds than state-of-the-art vector search systems.
The authors report that OneDB captures user intent effectively.

narrative_sequence.summary: Multi-modal data accumulation creates opportunities for data mining applications.
Effective retrieval is challenging because user retrieval intents are diverse and dynamic.
Existing vector search systems use static embeddings or fixed weights that fail to adapt to varying modality preferences.
OneDB addresses the gap with a distributed multi-metric similarity-search framework and three algorithmic innovations.
The authors report accuracy and retrieval-speed improvements on real-world datasets.

source_observation.claim: The system learns metric weights from limited query examples and tunes parameters for dynamic environments.

interpretation.claim: Combining lightweight preference learning with adaptive system tuning may help similarity search respond to changing retrieval intent.

application.claim: A multi-modal retrieval system could use small amounts of interaction data to personalize modality weighting and continuously adjust operational parameters.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish how much query data is needed, how preferences are represented, or whether adaptation remains effective under different workload conditions.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the real-world datasets, dataset sizes, or evaluation protocol.
The abstract does not identify the compared vector search systems or baseline configurations.
The abstract does not report resource costs, latency distributions, or adaptation overhead.
